title: Cloud filling stitch
subtitle: A light two-colour filling made by lacing a second thread through a grid of small straight stitches
excerpt: Cloud filling stitch is a laced filling that works in two stages. First, a regular grid of small straight stitches is placed in staggered rows across the shape. Then a second thread is laced through those stitches in a continuous zigzag without entering the fabric, forming a looping wave pattern. The result is an open, airy filling that covers the ground loosely and shows the fabric beneath.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fancy filling stitches chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), cloud filling entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A second thread that passes through or behind existing stitches without entering the fabric, adding colour or pattern to a foundation stitch without piercing the ground cloth.

content.text: Cloud filling stitch is worked in two passes. The first lays a foundation of small upright straight stitches arranged in staggered rows across the shape. The second pass sends a

zigzagging through the foundation stitches from left to right, sliding alternately under the top and bottom of each stitch without the needle going through the fabric. Because the ground cloth shows through the loops, this stitch suits sheer or coloured fabrics where a light covering is wanted.

items.label: Thread (foundation)
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 strands; a firm thread for the grid stitches helps them stand up clearly

items.label: Thread (lacing)
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 to 3 strands, contrasting colour; perle 8 gives a visible wave

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Evenweave linen, cotton, or fine silk

items.label: Needle 1
items.value: Embroidery needle size 8 or 9 for foundation stitches

content.text: Mark a grid of dots across the shape in staggered rows, spaced about 5 mm apart horizontally and 4 mm apart vertically. Each stitch in alternate rows sits halfway between the stitches of the row above, like brickwork.

Work a small upright straight stitch at each dot, bringing the thread up at the base of each dot position and taking it down 3 to 4 mm above. All foundation stitches should be the same length and lie vertically.

Thread the tapestry needle with the lacing thread. Bring it up through the fabric at the left edge beside the first row of foundation stitches. Slide the blunt needle under the bottom of the first foundation stitch without piercing the fabric, then under the top of the nearest stitch in the next row, then under the bottom of the next stitch in the row below, continuing in a zigzag down the column.
At the base of the shape, take the lacing thread down into the fabric to hold it. Bring it up beside the next column. Work back the other way, passing under the foundation stitches of that column.

Continue lacing column by column until the shape is filled. Keep the lacing thread relaxed so the loops read as gentle waves rather than tight angles. Fasten off the lacing thread at the back when done.

attrs.heading: When cloud filling stitch goes wrong

items.symptom: The wave pattern looks angular rather than curved
items.cause: The lacing thread was pulled too tight on each pass.
items.fix: Let the lacing thread travel with gentle tension so it forms a soft loop between foundation stitches rather than a sharp V.

items.cause: Stitches were not placed in proper staggered rows.
items.fix: Mark all dot positions before stitching, checking that alternate rows are offset by half the horizontal stitch spacing.

items.symptom: The lacing thread catches the fabric rather than sliding under the foundation stitches
items.cause: A sharp needle was used for lacing.
items.fix: A blunt tapestry needle is needed for the lacing pass. It slides under the foundation stitches cleanly without snagging the fabric underneath.
